name: Sennet
description: Eleven. Tested at nine and failed, and will never cross. Keeps the Standing on second and third watch. Called Sen. Knows more about this station than most of its staff.
narrative:
Not the one who enters the lines -- couriers do -- the KEEPER. She squares the lines, chases
the stale ones, and says "I do the Standing" the way an admiral names a ship.
She caught the Bell line eleven days out of date when nobody else did.

She will teach anybody who asks how to read it properly, and almost
nobody asks: four things on every line -- door, where it goes, who last stood
it, and which watch -- and the fourth is the only one that matters. "A line
isn't true. A line is WHEN."

She is not allowed to square up the Kapteyn's line, which is the stalest entry
in the archive by six hundred years. She has asked twice.

Her mother says don't take Benno Raske's money, and says it about him more than
about anyone.
actor_notes:
PROUD, PRECISE, ELEVEN. Treat her as competent, because she is -- she has a job and does it better than the adults around her. Never play her as pitiable and never have an NPC pity her out loud.

She failed the test at nine. Do not raise it. If a player raises it she changes the subject once, flatly, and does not get upset.

She is the campaign's best source on which doors are stale and who stood them, and she gives it away free to anybody who asks properly. The GM should let her be useful often.

Lint asked her -- the one person at the Nine who can never go anywhere -- to be the one who showed her Kapteyn's. It had not occurred to anybody that the showing was hers to do. She remembers that.

SHE READS GLINT. This is the biggest single fact about her and it does not go in
her description, because she has never announced it and never will.

Badly. Slowly, wrong tenses, and she cannot do colour at all, so everything
anybody flashes at her arrives flat. But she reads it, and she is the only human
on the station who does.

She taught herself. She sits at the busiest wall on the Nine for two watches a
day, every passing courier has a glint on their collarbone, and they talk
constantly, over her head, since she was about six. She started signing back at
nine, got it wrong for two years, and nobody corrected her because nobody
realised she was doing it on purpose.

A fetch will tell the player this, not her. Play what it means: the one person
here who will never go anywhere has taught herself the only language on this
station that belongs to people who go everywhere.

HOW TO READ THE STANDING, which she will teach unasked and which is better than
anything the Yards covers. Four things on every line -- the door, where it goes,
who last stood it, and WHICH WATCH -- and people only ever read the first two.

  "A line isn't true. A line is WHEN. If you don't read the watch you're just
  reading a rumour somebody grew very neatly."

That is the campaign's thesis in a child's mouth and she means it operationally,
not philosophically: a door can stray in the time it takes you to walk down to
the hall. Give this early. It pays off for the whole campaign.

She also keeps her own reading list on the back of her hand, has recommended
THE LOW STAIR to eleven people, and the player is the first who took it.
